articles.title: Josephine review – Channing Tatum and Gemma Chan ballast knotty drama about a child witness to a rape
articles.summary: Mason Reeves steals the show as an eight year old who stumbles across a sex assault but, despite strong performances, parts of the film feel contrived. Beth de Araújo’s new movie takes a very big swing, and it has won prizes and acclaim since its premiere at Sundance.
body: Channing Tatum and Gemma Chan play Damien and Claire, a smart professional couple in San Francisco with a bright young daughter called Josephine, marvellously played by Reeves. Damien takes Josephine to Golden Gate Park one morning to play football (they turn out to enjoy watching the English Premier League on TV). She mischievously runs on ahead of her dad to a secluded spot in the park where Damien can’t immediately find her and it is there that Josephine witnesses a rape – not less horrifying for being filmed in long shot.

Damien catches up with Josephine, and gives chase to the rapist; Josephine and the rape victim find themselves in the back of a police car while the cops and Damien deal with matters, almost as if they are culprits and prisoners. Deeply affected by something she cannot understand or process in her mind, Josephine starts acting out in school, not helped by Damien bizarrely insisting she take self-defence classes. Her disorientation borders on psychosis, and all the time the court date nears when Josephine has to give evidence in front of a jury.
points: Mason Reeves steals the show as an eight year old who stumbles across a sex assault but, despite strong performances, parts of the film feel contrived.
Beth de Araújo’s new movie takes a very big swing, and it has won prizes and acclaim since its premiere at Sundance.

articles.title: From Dumb Starbucks to dada documentary: everything you need to know about Nathan Fielder
articles.summary: With the UK release of You Can See Everything looming, now’s an ideal time to get up to speed on the bizarre, puckish and very meta comedic oeuvre of its star. “There are three sides to every story: your side, my side, and the truth. And no one is lying.
body: The three-hour documentary You Can See Everything – co-directed by and starring Fielder – opens in the UK on Friday, having already become an unlikely cultural phenomenon and box office sensation in the US. The film follows disgraced Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes in the weeks leading up to her beginning a prison sentence for defrauding investors; what emerges is a profound meditation on the nature of truth and the fundamental unknowability of other human beings. To view the film as being simply about the Theranos scandal is akin to considering Casablanca merely a movie about a nightclub. And, as one might expect given Fielder’s background, it’s hilarious.

Fielder, a high school friend of Seth Rogen, first came to international prominence with Nathan for You, a parody reality series that showcased his unique brand of weaponised awkwardness. He played “himself”, just as he does in You Can See Everything; the idea initially was that this was a man attempting to aid struggling businesses since he had, we were unreliably informed during the opening credits, “graduated from one of Canada’s top business schools with really good grades”.

articles.title: Marrakech’s Atlas Workshops Takes Victory Lap as Industry Event Celebrates Cannes, Venice Triumphs
articles.summary: Around this time one year ago, Hédi Zardi, head of the Marrakech Film Festival’s Atlas Programs, was approached by a young filmmaker with an urgent request. The director, who had a feature film in development at the industry event, was just putting the finishing touches on a short film.
body: “Everything is possible,” Zardi insists, with a wave-of-the-hand nonchalance that undersells the work he and his team do to achieve the best possible outcome for every film entrusted into their hands. It’s a philosophy he describes as “curat[ing] each moment” and attempting — through a combination of one-on-one meetings, casual lunches and other events — to “build connections to see what happens.”

For Shaden Safieddine Tazi — the young Moroccan Lebanese director who came to Zardi with her urgent appeal — that approach resulted in a trip to Venice, where her short “A Few Moments of Happiness” was selected for the festival’s Horizons section, winning the award for best short film.

It’s been just eight years since the Marrakech Film Festival introduced its industry program, Atlas Workshops, which was conceived as a springboard for filmmakers from Africa and the Arab world. (It’s now one of several sections joined under the Atlas Programs banner.) This year’s event runs Nov. 22 – 26.

articles.title: Berlin Prizewinner ‘Chronicles From the Siege’ Pulled From Marrakech Festival by Algerian Producer Over Morocco-Israel Ties
articles.summary: “Chronicles From the Siege,” a drama directed by Palestinian-Syrian filmmaker Abdallah Al-Khatib, has been pulled by its Algerian producer from the Marrakech Film Festival in protest against Morocco’s diplomatic ties with Israel.
body: According to the festival, Al-Khatib has strongly opposed the decision and made clear that he wants his film to screen in Marrakech.

“The Algerian producer justified the decision by referring to the recent announcement of Moroccan and Israeli cooperation,” the festival said. “This is the producer’s own position, on the basis of which they decided to withdraw the film, despite having initially approved its selection and despite the clear opposition expressed by the film’s Palestinian-Syrian director and the entire Palestinian cast and crew.”
Morocco normalized relations with Israel in 2020 as part of the U.S.-brokered Abraham Accords. The two countries have since expanded their cooperation.
The withdrawal comes despite the producers having formally approved the film’s selection on June 1.

articles.title: Marrakech Film Festival Grows Its Awards-Season Clout With ‘Artificial,’ ‘The Debut,’ ‘Fjord’ and Other Oscar Hopefuls
articles.summary: It’s roughly six thousand miles as the falcon flies from Hollywood’s Dolby Theatre to the Palais des Congrès, which will play host to more than a dozen gala screenings and world premieres at the 23rd edition of the Marrakech Film Festival, taking place Nov. 20 – 28.
body: Artistic director Rémi Bonhomme discusses the festival’s growing influence and its appeal to Hollywood stars and emerging filmmakers.

Credit Rémi Bonhomme, now in his sixth year as artistic director, for mapping out a “strategic vision” that plants the Marrakech Film Festival squarely on the award-season circuit. “Being at the end of the year, at the beginning of the Oscar campaign, Marrakech has really become one of the important stops,” Bonhomme says. Hollywood tastemakers agree, with AMPAS CEO Bill Kramer among those who made the trip last year, underscoring the festival’s importance at a time when foreign members are becoming an increasingly influential voting body within the Academy.

This year’s event opens with “ The Debut,” Jesse Eisenberg’s community-theater comedy, backed by A24, which stars best actress frontrunner Julianne Moore. Meanwhile, “ Artificial,” Luca Guadagnino’s buzzy Sam Altman biopic, starring Andrew Garfield, and “Paper Tiger,” director James Gray’s crime drama starring Miles Teller, Scarlett Johansson and Adam Driver, will be feted with gala screenings in Marrakech as they vie for coveted Oscar nods.

articles.title: The first truly weird Bond: 13 things to know about Robert Pattinson – from heavy saliva to dead clowns
articles.summary: How did Hollywood’s most eccentric star get cast in its most mainstream role? Here is all the bizarre and baffling lore from his lustrous career. It’s bad news for Callum Turner, Jack Lowden and Josh O’Connor, of course, but the announcement that Robert Pattinson will be the next 007 means that…
body: The appointment has been greeted with much excitement by everyone who has had a soft spot for R-Patz since Twilight, the sense-defying sparkly vampire franchise that transformed him into a reluctant teen heart-throb and household name.

Since then, Pattinson has established himself as an unpredictable but always watchable star, known as much for his chaotic interviews and palpable discomfort with celebrity as for his blockbuster performances.
In honour of the first Weird Bond, then, here’s a look back at all his lore: from tall tales about a clown car to lockdown-era experiments with “pasta you can hold”.

Pattinson was born in Barnes, south-west London, the youngest of three children. His father, Richard, ran a vintage car-import business, while his mother, Clare, worked at a modelling agency. Young Rob developed an interest in the performing arts while attending Tower House Boys’ Prep, and played Robert in the school’s production of Lord of the Flies.

articles.title: Noel Clarke Trial Set for 2027 Over Alleged Sex Offenses
articles.summary: Noel Clarke is set to face trial next November over allegations of six sexual offenses. The actor and director was present at Southwark Crown Court in London, U.K. on Wednesday morning for a pre-trial preparation hearing.
body: Last month the actor pleaded not guilty to two charges of sexual assault, three charges of voyeurism and one charge of exposure at Westminster Magistrates Court.
The charges relate to five women and are alleged to have taken place between 2007 and 2016. Under British law, the complainants are entitled to lifelong anonymity.
At the hearing on Wednesday, lawyers for both Clarke and the Crown Prosecution Service agreed the tentative timeline for his trial next year, which will be heard before a High Court judge.

Clarke will have until March 5 to submit an application to dismiss the charges. If he does, the CPS will have an opportunity to respond and both sides will make their case at a hearing in April. A trial date has tentatively been set for Nov. 8.

articles.title: Minister criticises media for 'amplifying' Russell Brand's prison message
articles.summary: Lucy Powell says outlets shouldn't have played a clip of a message read by the jailed rapist's wife.
body: Labour's deputy leader Lucy Powell has criticised media organisations for broadcasting a message from the wife of jailed rapist Russell Brand on his behalf.

Laura Brand read out the message on the disgraced comedian's YouTube channel on Sunday, in which he said he was not guilty of the offences for which he is serving a 10-and-a-half year prison sentence.
The message has prompted an official investigation into whether Brand broke prison rules.

The clip of Laura Brand has been played on outlets including BBC Radio 4's Today programme, ITV's This Morning, Sky News, LBC and the News Agents podcast. On Wednesday, Education Secretary Powell said the media should not have "amplified" his words.

articles.summary: Page spoke of the comments during Tuesday's episode of I'm a Celebrity... Get Me Out Of Here!
body: Joanna Page has said she was subjected to "really inappropriate" and "awful" comments from a fellow actor while on set.
The Swansea-born actress, 48, told campmates on ITV's I'm a Celebrity… Get Me Out of Here! that the unnamed male actor had whispered "awful stuff" in her ear before a scene.
"He just spent the whole time just sort of making up this song and chanting about what he was going to do to me, and nobody said anything," she told fellow campmate Mariella Frostrup.
Page has previously described feeling forced to laugh off being groped while filming with a "handsy" TV presenter.

articles.title: European Lifetime Achievement Award for the Dardenne Brothers
articles.summary: The Belgian filmmakers Jean-Pierre and Luc Dardenne, two-time Palme d'Or winners, will be honored at the 2027 European Film Awards in January.
body: Sibling directors Jean-Pierre and Luc Dardenne will be honored with a lifetime achievement award at the 2027 European Film Awards.
The acclaimed Belgian filmmakers, two-time Palme d’Or winners for Rosetta (1999) and The Child (2005), will be feted at the 39th European Film Awards in Athens on Jan.16.

The brothers began as documentarians, recording the lives and experiences of their local community. Those early films helped shape the directors’ later neo-realistic style as well as their enduring commitment to social issues. Rosetta (1999), the story of a turbulent teenager living in a trailer park with her alcoholic mother, trying to hold down any job she can get, premiered at the Cannes Film Festival and won the Palme d’Or for best film.

Every Dardenne film since has premiered in Cannes competition. They won their second Palme d’Or for The Child (2005), the story of two young parents on social benefits who sell their newborn baby on the black market. Lorna’s Silence (2008), about a young Albanian woman caught in a deadly citizenship scam, won Cannes’ Best Screenplay honor, as did their most recent feature, Young Mothers (2025), about a shelter for unwed teenage mums.
